text: Ten fourteen, Tuesday morning. Branch services are slowing down.
And nobody has opened a ticket yet.
Part two: from the first symptom to a closed ticket, end to end.
Detect, enrich, ticket, notify. Levels one and two are automated.
Level three keeps a human in the loop.
So who owns this incident?
Machines handle levels one and two. People decide at level three.
IBM SevOne. From incident, to resolution.
Step one: detect and enrich.
A failing optic triggers twenty-three alerts. SevOne correlates them into one incident.
ITAM and the CMDB add the asset, the owner group, and the business service.
Card payments. Tier one. Under support contract, with the last change on record.
Step two: the ticket.
SevOne opens a ServiceNow incident in six seconds.
Configuration item, priority, assignment group, and evidence, filled in automatically.
One ticket, not twenty-three, and it stays in sync both ways.
Step three: notify and route.
NetOps South is paged in Teams. DevSecOps gets the agent change in Slack.
The service owner is told what to expect.
The policy is clear: levels one and two run automatically.
Level three needs a human.
Step four: levels one and two.
Level one triages, and fails traffic over to the backup path.
Service is restored in forty-seven seconds. Nobody was paged to fix it.
Level two finds the failing optic, opens the vendor case, and reserves a spare from ITAM.
The hardware swap is a risky change. It escalates to level three.
Step five: the human in the loop.
A level three engineer reviews the evidence, and approves the change.
After the swap, SevOne verifies zero loss, and the incident closes itself, with ITAM updated.
Machines handle levels one and two.
People decide at level three.
IBM SevOne. From incident, to resolution.
